    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors.
    • Lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly. If you're not a fellow pessimist, proceed with caution.

    Recent findings suggest that the Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors. They failed to hit 100 points against the Kings and their 28th-ranked defense. They managed just 87 at Golden State.

    Lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league). Only 25.6% of their shots are at the rim, the fourth-fewest in the league per Cleaning the Glass, and no team takes fewer shots per game from inside the restricted area.

    In a recent development, they are about as extreme a jump-shooting team as you will find, and right now the shots are not going in. Over these last four, the Celtics have made just 28% of their 3s and 38% of their overall shots. Throw in 65% from the free-throw line and those are all bottom-two marks over that span, plus the 389 points they scored is the lowest over any four-game stretch since 2012 for a Boston offense.

    It's not just the number of 3s the Celtics rely, sometimes more than others, it's the kinds of 3s. Every team wants the shots off ball and player movement, drives and kicks, drawing two and swinging, but when the Celtics aren't able to create the initial leverage by attacking the rim (they don't have to do this with just drives; they aim to do so by cutting and rolling, too), they end up taking more pull-up 3s than any team in the league, both as a total number and percentage of their overall shot diet.

    Those are traditionally tougher shots, and indeed Boston is making them at a 33.5% clip. The Celtics also don't generate a ton of the coveted corner 3s (which are often a result of rim pressure) relative to their volume, and thus take more above-the-break 3s than any team. There are also a lot of one-on-one 3s; only the Lakers and Timberwolves take more 3s after three or more dribbles, and the Celtics make those at only 29%.

    Sources indicate that bottom line, Derrick White is shooting 28% from 3 for the year and has missed 22 of his last 25 from deep (he had so many premium looks against Golden State and they just will not go in for him). Payton Pritchard has missed 21 of his last 29 from deep. Jayson Tatum is having a stellar all-around season and is leveraging his scoring attention to find teammates more effectively than ever, but quietly his shooting is in the dumps, too.

    According to recent reports, tatum is shooting 42.6% overall and 33.6% from 3, both of which would be career lows if you discard the 15 games he played last season after returning ahead of schedule from the Achilles tear. Tatum has never been a particularly adept pull-up 3-point shooter, for which he'll probably always be prone to settling to at least some degree. Tatum's pull-up 3s over his last four full seasons:.

    According to recent reports, any team that launches as many 3s as the Celtics is going to endure some extreme ebbs and flows, and coach Joe Mazzulla remains committed to the course. "... If we're getting good shots, which more times than not we are, you have to be able to trust over the course of a season that that's going to work out," he mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that the truth is, the Celtics don't really have a choice other than to trust the shots to go in. They don't have a strategy B to speak of. They don't get to the rim and they don't have a post presence. They have a gang of good shooters, but that doesn't guarantee good shooting.

    In a recent development, the Celtics rely on getting more shots than their opponents by winning the turnover and offensive-rebounding battles, which they generally do, but as Mazzulla also remarked, "at some point you have to knock [the shots] down. That's just not happening right now.".

    After Harden scored 51 against the Pacers last Friday, Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson did the increasingly cliché "we've got to appreciate this guy" dance while calling Harden a "top 10 of all-time" player.

    Sources indicate that kenny Atkinson after James Harden's 51-point game: "We've got to appreciate this guy. This guy is top 10 of all-time." pic.twitter.com/YUt2Y6pQYL.

    Remember, Atkinson is the guy who told reporters: "Analytically … we've won two out of three" right before the Cavaliers got swept by the Knicks in last year's Eastern Conference Finals. That was kind of overblown, to be fair. He was simply citing the types of shots the Cavs got vs. the ones the Knicks got, and that getting the right shots is a recipe for success more often than not, which every coach from the beginning of time has believed.

    Atkinson just would've been better off if he'd gone the "make or miss league" route. Once you start invoking analytical results over actual results, you're going to get rightfully roasted as the number nerd that you are.

    Through this lens, it makes sense that Atkinson thinks Harden is a top 10 all-time player. Numbers-wise, he's ninth all-time with almost 30,000 career points. He's 11th in assists and, barring injury, will almost surely pass Isiah Thomas for 10th by the end of the season. Only Stephen Curry has made more 3-pointers than Harden, who's piled up so many numbers he's actually top 20 all-time in steals.

    None of this adds up to top 10.

    Industry observers note that of course this is subjective, but this is my Hater Report, so allow me to hate. Harden was a manipulating machine of egregious proportions. I'm not saying he wasn't a great scorer, or even that he sometimes still isn't. Two things can indeed be true. But if we're going to start throwing around top 10, we're sure as hell going to factor heavily the conditions under which you dominated.

    Harden played in the NBA's version of the steroid era. It was juiced up on some level for every scorer, but nobody mastered the dark arts like Harden, who cheated his way to so many phony fouls that guys were literally starting to guard him with their hands behind their backs.

    Industry observers note that now listen, before you start with the "he wasn't breaking any rules" nonsense, keep in mind that steroids weren't technically illegal in baseball when Barry Bonds' head looked like it was going to pop. Harden scammed his way to more points than anyone in history. The flops and flails were impossible to stomach or, more importantly, defend against. Falling down on damn near every 3-pointer he took actually became part of his follow-through. I would only be mildly surprised if you hid a camera in his private workouts if he wasn't falling down in an empty gym, because he was so used to doing it.

    This created more than just a gazillion free throws; it created a scoring environment in which Harden could operate against defenders who were way more frightened of fouling than being scored on. It was as if he was being perpetually defended by guys with five fouls.

    Sources indicate that now account for the one-man-show usage. I remember Raja Bell once telling me there are way more players than you think who could score 25 points per game if given the opportunity. Hell, Darius Acuff Jr. is doing it right now and until a week ago, he was a teenager.

    Industry observers note that that's not to say anyone could do what Harden did, but given his set of circumstances, it's irresponsible to call him one of the 10 greatest players ever on numbers alone. Back in 2022, ESPN ranked him 50th all time, which feels much closer to reality, and he's only gotten worse since then.

    I mean, just start rattling names off the top of your head. Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant, Wilt Chamberlain, Larry Bird, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Hakeem Olajuwon, Kobe Bryant, Tim Duncan, Shaquille O'Neal. We're already at 12 and there's not even a debate with any of them.

    Recent findings suggest that no coach in his right mind would take Harden over Nikola Jokić, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Kevin Garnett, Karl Malone, Scottie Pippen, Charles Barkley, Isiah Thomas, Dwyane Wade or prime Chris Paul. I never watched Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Julius Erving, Moses Malone, Elgin Baylor or some guy named Bill Russell, but something tells me the vast majority of coaches are taking those guys over Harden, too.

    According to recent reports, it bears repeating that none of this means to suggest Harden hasn't been an all-time player. He's a first-ballot Hall of Famer. He's not an empty-stats guy by any stretch; he led a team that very possibly would've won the championship in the middle of Golden State's dynasty were it not for a Chris Paul injury. But there are levels to this, and trying to elevate Harden into the top one on the strength of gaudy numbers in an absolutely juiced-up era of his game would be like trying to call Sammy Sosa one of the greatest hitters ever. It's just not even close to true.

    Industry observers note that back in 2021, I called Young an average shooter who thinks he's Stephen Curry and got absolutely roasted for it. Turns out, I wasn't harsh enough on Young, whose shooting has been consistently deteriorating to the point that he is now a flat-out bad shooter. Even with a 7-for-15 run from 3 over his last two games, which at this point is a downright nuclear stretch for him, Young is shooting 32.5% from 3 and a pitiful 36.4% overall.

    The fact that he's among the league leaders in assists means almost nothing; passing has always been his one elite gift (it goes largely hand in hand with his former ability to breach the paint at will), but it comes at the hefty cost of him controlling the ball for almost the same amount of time per possession as Luka Dončić this season. Just because those two were traded for one another doesn't mean they are, or ever have been, anywhere near the same caliber of player.

    It has been revealed that even at his peak when he was one of the league's better shot generators, it was debatable whether you could justify sponsoring Young's personal dribbling show with your offense, let alone paying him max money given the defensive trade-off. But now that he can't shoot or beat anyone off the dribble, that $212 million deal the Wizards gifted him this summer, which was a disaster the moment the ink dried, somehow looks even worse.

    According to recent reports, washington is trying to salvage some sort of value from Young. They're starting to take him off the ball some, which, given the good shooting the last few games, is going to give the apologists hope. Don't fall for it. The numbers, not just this year but going back a long time, speak for themselves.

    According to recent reports, there's a difference between a talented shooter and a good one. Young fooled people with range and confidence for a while, and he had an unearned marksman reputation that died hard. But the jig is up. This is an average shooter at best, and he's rarely at his best.

    After losing four straight games by 20-plus while also being held under 100 points in each (an equation of futility that goes unmatched by any other team this century), the Warriors finally got their first win since losing Curry to an oblique tear by beating the aforementioned ice-cold Celtics.

    Sources indicate that it certainly wasn't because of their offense. The Warriors were once again held to double digits, managing just 88 points. Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors, who register a top-five offense with Curry, have scraped together an anemic 96.2 points per 100 possessions on 48.5% true-shooting, both being the worst marks in the league by a laughable margin.

    According to recent reports, over this five-game stretch, the Warriors have been outscored by 108 points. The 1997-98 team that also lost four straight by at least 20 points was a minus-104 over that stretch. That was the season that Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo, mind you. The Warriors won 19 games. That's the kind of firm these Warriors are trolling in right now.

    If Curry doesn't get back soon, we might have to start worrying about Draymond Green putting Steve Kerr in a full nelson.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The New York Mets gave Tarik Skubal a record nine-year, $450 million contract Sunday evening and the case can be made that it was only the second-best contract they gave out this past weekend. On Saturday, the Mets locked up center fielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year extension worth $95 million, with a club option for a ninth year. The 22-year-old Ewing is now signed through 2034.

    It has been revealed that there was certainly no urgency on the part of the Mets to lock up Ewing, who would not have become a free agent until after the 2032 season. There might have been urgency on Ewing's part, however. First and foremost, he secured life-changing money after only five months in the major leagues. I will never ever begrudge a player for signing an early career extension.

    It has been revealed that second, the collective bargaining agreement will expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and MLB's various proposals have included not only a salary cap, but also contract limits. The league proposed a maximum five-year contract at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, and six years at 16% of the cap for players who stay with their team.

    Ewing's extension may not be possible under the next CBA. That's a pretty good reason to sign a deal now, and it may incentivize other young players to sign long-term extensions between now and the CBA's expiration next week. Here now are 10 players who could get an extension done under the wire this week.

    It has been revealed that the Brewers aggressively lock up their best young players, including signing Luis Lara and Cooper Pratt to long-term deals even before they made their MLB debuts this summer. Misiorowski, the reigning National League Cy Young winner, could qualify as a Super Two, meaning he would go through arbitration four times rather than the usual three. The Cy Young and All-Star Games will boost his arbitration salaries significantly. It might not be long before he gets priced out of Milwaukee. If nothing else, it would behoove the Brewers to touch base with Misiorowski's representatives and see whether they can find common ground this week.

    Sources indicate that because they can afford big arbitration salaries and avoid the inherent risk that comes with long-term contracts, the Yankees do not give out early career extensions often. Perhaps they'll make an exception for Schlittler, who won the American League Cy Young unanimously and now leads a rotation that includes three high-priced veterans (Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón). Keep in mind that Schlittler was a seventh-round draft pick who received a $205,000 signing bonus. He's still waiting for his first big payday and might jump at a team-friendly extension to secure life-changing money.

    Industry observers note that although Munetaka Murakami got the attention, Vargas was the White Sox's best player in 2026. He offers a rare blend of power (33 home runs), patience (101 walks), and contact (126 strikeouts, a good total in this era). His third base defense has improved from poor to passable, which still isn't great, but is at least playable. There's no more talk about a permanent move to first base or even DH. Vargas just turned 27 and he's three years away from free agency. The White Sox are a team on the rise and making sure Vargas will be around beyond his team control years would be a tidy bit of business before the newly introduced CBA kicks in.

    Free agent after: 2031 for both.

    In a recent development, benge and McLean finished second and fourth in NL Rookie of the Year voting, respectively, and like Ewing, they are the homegrown pieces who will supplement the well-paid veterans like Skubal and Juan Soto. I am certain the Mets and president of baseball operations David Stearns have at least broached long-term extensions with both Benge and McLean, and maybe something will get done with one or both between now and the CBA's expiration. My sense is the Mets would like Ewing's deal to be the first of several extensions with their foundational young players, not a one-off.

    Industry observers note that the NL Rookie of the Year really fills up the box score and has the skill set that will balloon his arbitration salaries. Home runs, RBI, etc. That all pays very well in arbitration and the Reds may want to get out in front of it, and lock in Stewart at a discounted rate that nonetheless pays him well and gives him a nice payday. The Reds tried and failed to extend Elly De La Cruz last offseason, according to The Athletic. That ship may have already sailed. Stewart, though, might be more open to the idea.

    Free agent after: 2031 for Messick and 2032 for Bazzana.

    It was under then-GM John Hart in the 1990s that Cleveland pioneered the practice of locking up young players to team-friendly extensions. Manny Ramirez, Jim Thome, and others signed deals when they were years away from free agency. They got paid and the team gained cost control over their arbitration years, plus a free agent year or two. Bazzana and Messick -- Gavin Williams as well -- are next in line for long-term contracts. Messick was the AL Rookie of the Year runner-up and the third-place finisher for the AL Cy Young. That will reward him come arbitration time. Bazzana, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2024 Draft, has yet to fully launch, but that's typically when the Guardians get down to business. They like to lock players up before they break out.

    Under POBO Craig Breslow, the Red Sox have aggressively locked up their top young players, and it's been a mixed bag. There's been some good (Ceddanne Rafaela), some bad (Brayan Bello and Kristian Campbell), and some TBD (Roman Anthony). Tolle figures to be next in line for an extension. He's excellent and this year's third-place finish in the AL Rookie of the Year voting figures to be the first of many awards votes Tolle receives in the coming years. The Bello and Campbell deals going sour shouldn't dissuade the Red Sox from trying to extend Tolle between now and the CBA's expiration.

    Sources indicate that I think the Tigers and Dingler learned a little something about managing his workload in 2026. They rode him hard this year. Dingler started 80 of the team's first 92 games, came off the bench five other times, and frequently DHed when he wasn't behind the plate. Not coincidentally, Dingler went from an .831 OPS in the first half to a .631 OPS in the second half. The man's legs must have been jello. Anyway, Dingler looks the part of a franchise catcher both at the plate and behind it, and good young catchers are always worth keeping. The Tigers recently extended Troy Melton. My guess is they'll try to extend Dingler soon too.

    Not long after fortifying their rotation with the signing of Trevor Rogers, the Chicago Cubs have struck again by landing slugger Teruaki Soto out of Japan on a six-year, $120 million contract, ESPN reports.

    It has been revealed that earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Sato, who turns 28 in March, as the No. 4 free agent of the current 2026-27 class. Here's part of our write-up:.

    Recent findings suggest that "He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact concerns to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.".

    Sources indicate that sato is expected to play a corner outfield spot for the Cubs even though he's a corner infielder by trade. He does, however, have significant time in the outfield, where the Cubs are in need of help after the incumbent corner outfielders, Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, departed in free agency. In 2026, Suzuki and Happ combined for a WAR of 7.8, so the bar for Sato will be relatively high when it comes to replacing a chunk of that value.

    In a recent development, in addition to the $120 million contract owed to Sato, the Cubs also must pay Sato's former team, the Hanshin Tigers, a posting fee. For contracts in excess of $50 million, the posting agreement between MLB and NPB mandates that the posting fee will be 20% of the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the next $25 million plus 15% of the total guaranteed value exceeding $50 million. In the Cubs' case, that comes to a bit more than $20 million they'll owe Hanshin.

    In a recent development, the Cubs are coming off a 2026 season in which they won 89 games and earned a postseason berth as the second-place team in the National League Central. In the playoffs, though, they were swept out of the Wild Card Series by the San Diego Padres in two games.

    Recent findings suggest that from one future Pro Football Hall of Famer to another, Tom Brady was disappointed by Aaron Rodgers' comments this week leading to his release from the Pittsburgh Steelers. After the team revealed it was benching Rodgers for Mason Rudolph on Tuesday night ahead of Friday's game against the Denver Broncos, Rodgers publicly lashed out at coach Mike McCarthy, embarrassing him on a national stage.

    Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings, not being on task on the job and failing to connect with players. Brady said "nobody wins when the family feuds" and disagreed with how Rodgers handled the situation.

    Recent findings suggest that "In response to that, the sanctity of an NFL locker room is a very sacred place, and we should never lose track of that as players," Brady stated during the second half of Thursday's Eagles-Cowboys game. "It's a privilege to be in that locker room. You're fighting with your teammates. You're fighting coaches. You're always acting as a team together. It shouldn't always be the place for private things to become public; that's what I'll say.".

    Brady, who went 3–2 in his career against the former longtime Green Bay Packers quarterback, including a 31–26 victory in the 2021 NFC Championship Game, said Rodgers' admissions were selfish given his role on the team.

    "Certainly a Hall of Fame career, and he's a tremendous player, and it has nothing to do with his play style," Brady mentioned. "I was fortunate to be around a lot of great teammates over the years, and what made a great teammate to me was, you cared about your teammates and your coaches and you cared about what the team was trying to accomplish.

    "And that supersedes any individual aspect of your game that you want to promote. I was in a great locker room. I played for my teammates, I played for my coaches.".

    McCarthy took the high road hours after Rodgers' remarks this week.

    Recent findings suggest that "He has a lot of opinions, and there's things we've always talked about. I considered those private conversations," McCarthy said before Friday's game with the Broncos. "There's a long history there. Clearly [a] difference of opinion.".

    McCarthy and Rodgers were part of a braintrust in Green Bay that lasted 13 seasons, including a Super Bowl XLV victory in 2011. McCarthy remarked his only focus this week was beating the Broncos and said this team had the "opportunity to grow today because of the things that were said" from Rodgers.

    "And all those teammates have to — they're going to go and regroup, and that's going to hopefully galvanize them toward, you know, you feel like you're in the foxhole together," Brady said.

    Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin called the dispute between Rodgers and McCarthy a "dumpster fire" and expressed "general sadness" that the relationship between professionals would end this way.

    Recent findings suggest that "Sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career in the quarterback Aaron Rodgers, and just at the macro level whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum," Tomlin mentioned Wednesday on The Pat McAfee Show. "Those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football.".

    #222396. Industry News: Why asking Trae Young to score less is a band-aid, not a fix for the Wizards' self-inflicted problem

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1182 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why asking Trae Young to score less is a band-aid, not a fix for the Wizards' self-inflicted problem

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Washington Wizards entered Tuesday with a 7-11 record.
    • Recent findings suggest that in Washington's first 15 games, he averaged around 6.6 minutes of possession per game, tied for the third-most in the league.
    • Young, 28, has been a mess as a scorer this season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Washington Wizards entered Tuesday with a 7-11 record. In their seven wins, Trae Young is averaging just under 11.3 shot attempts per game. In those 11 losses, he's averaging 13.3. It's a small difference, but a notable one. The Wizards came into play Tuesday on a three-game winning streak, and a meaningful part of that streak has been Young spending less time on the ball.

    Recent findings suggest that in Washington's first 15 games, he averaged around 6.6 minutes of possession per game, tied for the third-most in the league. He's down to 4.5 in his last three games. He's dribbling around one fewer time per touch, and his average possession per touch is down around a second. These aren't glaring changes, but they've been helpful ones. It's not a coincidence, for example, that No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa's two best offensive games have come in this stretch.

    Young, 28, has been a mess as a scorer this season. He's shooting just 36.4% from the floor and 32.5% on 3s. He's barely getting to the basket and struggling mightily when he's in the paint. He can't beat defenders nearly as easily off the dribble as he once could. Getting the ball out of his hands a bit more has been essential.

    Industry observers note that it's been an intentional shift on Washington's part. Wizards officials have asked Young to focus less on his own scoring and instead emphasize his playmaking, according to The Athletic. Washington certainly won't complain about a 24-to-7 assist-to-turnover ratio in that stretch. Young, despite his noticeable decline as a scorer, remains a stellar passer. That's typically how star decline works. It comes in bits and pieces. Even as essential components of a player's game degrade, years of accumulated basketball IQ allow him to continue finding ways to contribute. After years of abject tanking, the Wizards seemingly wanted an offensive organizer around to help give their younger players some structure. Young can still do that.

    It has been revealed that but we're in an increasingly financially unforgiving NBA, and the Wizards aren't paying Young a contributor's salary. They're paying him star money, and they chose to do so after just five relatively quiet games with him a season ago. His four-year, $212 million max contract will pay him at the top of the market through the end of Dybantsa's rookie deal. With Anthony Davis on the books through the end of Kyshawn George and Alex Sarr's rookie deals, the Wizards effectively traded the roster-building flexibility those cheap rookie deals afforded them for two declining stars.

    It has been revealed that davis has justified the investment, at least as an asset. They haven't extended him. They could potentially flip him for more than they paid him. Young has not.

    And that's the dilemma the Wizards are now in.

    Clearly, less Young leads to more winning for the Wizards. But getting enough out of him to justify that enormous contract almost certainly requires more than they're currently getting. The entire value proposition of employing Young rests on him being a high-usage offensive engine. He just doesn't provide enough off-ball offensive value to justify what he gives up defensively at a max price point.

    Industry observers note that take his shooting, for example. "Trae's got so much gravity," Wizards coach Brian Keefe told The Athletic. "When he plays off the ball, he's going to draw people, and then we're getting into actions with him on the second side that have been really good." There's something to this in theory, especially since gravity tends to rest more on reputation than reality. But Young has never been a consistently reliable catch-and-shoot player. He's averaging less than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game this season and has made around 28% of them. He's never averaged more than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game in a season.

    Industry observers note that maybe he improves if his role demands more of these shots, but this is his ninth NBA season. That sort of shift this late in a career is rare.

    In a recent development, it's a daunting change. Young spent most of his seven-and-a-half-year Atlanta Hawks run as almost entirely an on-ball player. He's never scored more than 39 points off of cuts in a single season. He has none this season. He's never been an especially active mover or screener, and even if he's grown on that front over the last few years, that's from a starting point of essentially zero. Asking Young to be less of a heliocentric shot creator is essentially asking Young to be a different player entirely.

    In a recent development, that was the danger in paying Young sight unseen. They had no idea how he'd fit on this roster when they ponied up a max deal. If he'd picked up his player option and made this a prove-it season, they could have worked out the kinks and tried to sign him to a more appropriate deal next summer. The obvious argument here is that Young might have left had the Wizards refused to give him a long-term extension, but the counter here is that the Wizards would almost certainly have been better off if that had happened.

    Stephen Noh's salary model estimates that Young is worth $26.3 million so far this season. That's a bit less than half of what he's getting. If that persists over the life of the deal, it's among the NBA's worst contracts. If his scoring continues to decline as he loses burst with age, it's a borderline crisis. Young may remain a passing genius, but passing skill is not a one-to-one match with passing value. It's easier to set teammates up when you're a dangerous enough scorer to consistently draw help. If Young isn't generating the same sort of advantages he once did, the passes that were once available to him suddenly become harder.

    According to recent reports, all of this puts the Wizards in an extremely precarious long-term position. They had to get the ball out of Young's hands more in the present. Too much of their offense involved players more important to the organization's long-term looks -- Dybantsa chief among them -- watching him dribble. A lower-usage Young probably makes the Wizards a better team simply by spreading usage to players who need more of it.

    Sources indicate that but that doesn't mean that a lower-usage Young is especially valuable. On-ball creation is where much of Young's value is generated. His scoring has declined so much that he's not generating the same value he used to, so all of this has stuck the Wizards between a rock and a hard place. They can try to maximize Young's skill set at the expense of everyone else, or they can try to maximize the team as a whole. But in doing so, they're not getting nearly enough out of a player they're paying to be a centerpiece. The latter is probably the right decision, but it's still a choice between two bad options. It's a band-aid on a self-inflicted wound.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Snyder's Soapbox: Until MLB owners open the books, there's no reason to listen to pleas of poverty

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis.
    • The world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason.
    • Sources indicate that people are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Snyder's Soapbox! Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis. Some of the topics will be pressing matters, some might seem insignificant in the grand scheme of things, and most will be somewhere in between. The good thing about this website is that it's free, and you are allowed to click away. If you stay, you'll get smarter, though. That's a money-back guarantee. Let's get to it.

    The world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason. Obviously. We know all about that pesky CBA expiration on Dec. 1 and we know that the owners are all but certain to lock the players out that night while they push for a salary cap in the name of parity.

    Sources indicate that people are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side. They are the talent and why we watch the games. No one is buying owners' jerseys and sitting in the ballpark facing the suites.

    Another reason I'm not a huge fan, in general, of the owners is that I don't believe we're ever getting the full truth about how much money they make. The Braves are publicly traded and we can see a good breakdown of how they fared in 2025. The short version is that they are swimming in money. We could look at the two recently sold MLB teams for a hint, too. The Angels were sold for $4 billion; Arte Moreno bought the team for $184 million in 2003. The Padres were also sold recently for $3.9 billion. The San Diego media market size ranks ahead of only Kansas City, Cincinnati, Milwaukee and, eventually, Las Vegas among MLB cities.

    Sources indicate that and, again, sometimes you'll have an owner say the quiet part out loud. Enter Orioles owner David Rubenstein:.

    "A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," Rubenstein said last month at a forum with other pro sports owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C.

    Recent findings suggest that " ... I couldn't figure out why it is that people who are fans are so obsessed with the success of their local team. They're not going to make any more money. They're not going to go to the Super Bowl and get a trophy out of it.".

    People who cape for the owners: this is what you are defending.

    It has been revealed that obviously every owner shouldn't be painted with the same brush. Some of them are legitimately fans. But I'd be willing to wager pretty heavily that a majority of the owners think like Rubenstein here and view the teams simply as vehicles to make as much money as possible.

    Do we even need to bother with the suggestion that we shouldn't care about our favorite teams since they don't make us money and we don't get pieces of metal trophies? Sports fandom can be one of the purest and most wholesome things about our society. It brings families and friends together. It gives us emotions we otherwise couldn't even possibly imagine feeling. And I'll say this, too: I've seen my favorite team win the World Series and the absolute last thing on my mind was, "man, I'd sure like a trophy for my own mantle." The memories can't be matched by anything material at all. I would take nothing of real, tangible substance over those memories.

    It's maddening that an owner can be so out of touch with the product that he purchased.

    Do please hone in on the money comment, though. That's a much bigger deal. We've heard owners of some smaller-market teams cry poor for years and even decades, and the response from the MLBPA every single time is a pretty simple one. I reached out to a source and heard it again: "If any team wants us to believe they are losing money, they can simply open their books.".

    Yes. The Braves have to and we can see how much of a money machine they are in the 11th-ranked media market (counting the two-team cities twice).

    Again, there will be exceptions, but the owners generally just view their teams as virtual ATMs, the output of which would be even higher with artificially decreased payroll because of a salary cap. At least one of them doesn't even understand why we care as much as we do.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, after missing out on bigger name free agent starting pitchers like Tarik Skubal, Trevor Rogers, and Freddy Peralta, the Toronto Blue Jays have fortified their rotation by signing free agent right-hander Kaima Taira out of Japan. The deal is for $80 million over five years with an opt-out after the third year, the Newly introduced York Post reports.

    Sources indicate that earlier this offseason, CBS Sports ranked the undersized Taira as the No. 19 free agent of the current 2026-27 class. Here's part of that write-up:.

    "Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Seibu declared on Oct. 30 that Taira will be posted this offseason.".

    For his NPB career, Taira has a 1.85 ERA with 676 strikeouts in 633 ⅔ innings in a mix of rotation and bullpen duty. While, as noted above, Taira may not profile as a starter in MLB, the Jays will likely give him every opportunity to stick in their rotation, given their need there behind ace Dylan Cease. In addition to the $80 million commitment to Taira, the Jays will owe his former team, the Seibu Lions, a posting fee per the MLB-NPB agreement.

    Toronto won the pennant in 2025 but backslid in 2026 to 83 losses and a last-place finish in the American League East. The offense was their leading liability last season, but the rotation also needed attention. That explains why they were very much in the bidding for Skubal and other premium starting pitchers on the market. It furthermore explains why they're willing to take a chance on Taira.

    Welcome to the 12th of 17 weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy football fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until fantasy championships.

    In a recent development, as a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

    Industry observers note that belated Happy Thanksgiving, Happy Holidays and enjoy your weekend! Without further ado, here is my list for Week 12 of the 2026 season.

    After starting the year extremely hot, Bryce Young has cooled significantly over the last five weeks. And that cooldown started in Week 7 with a home game against the Buccaneers, who tagged him for two interceptions and a forced fumble, and held him to 163 yards and just one touchdown. His 7.42 fantasy points from that game remain his lowest output of the season and the outlook isn't much better in the Week 12 rematch.

    In a recent development, young will now be traveling into Raymond James Stadium, where the Bucs have allowed just 11.5 points per game to opposing QBs this year, in prime time, where Young has averaged just 12.56 fantasy points per game in five career contests. No matter which poison you pick, and there are several options, the situation is not great for Young heading into Tampa Bay this Monday night. With zero teams on bye, there are plenty of preferable streamers available. Go with one of those guys.

    What to do ❓ You should be able to bench Young for alternative options like Kirk Cousins, Deshaun Watson, J.J. McCarthy or even Jacoby Brissett.

    In a recent development, look, I can already hear the objections. Pollard has scored double-digit fantasy points in four straight games and averaged 23.3 PPG over that span. That includes the game two weeks ago, when he scored 19.9 against Jacksonville. So why would we fade him in the rematch? Well, let's dig into that stretch a little. He has scored fewer points in each successive game over that month, culminating in just 11.0 against the Cowboys last week, due to zero catches and no touchdown. And in that Jaguars game in particular, he managed just 33 rushing yards on nine carries, but salvaged his day with a career-high eight catches, one of which went for a 32-yard, fourth-quarter touchdown. That single play alone accounted for nearly 50% of his fantasy points on the day. The Jags remain the toughest run defense in the league — allowing the fewest rushing yards per game to running backs — and I don't foresee the same pass-catching parachute saving Pollard in this one. That makes him a major risk with a single-digit floor.

    Industry observers note that what to do ❓ Pollard is still a fringe RB2 on the merits of volume, but he's closer to the range of Zach Charbonnet or Chris Rodriguez Jr. (if Bhayshul Tuten is out) than he is to the top 15.

    Admittedly, you'd need some impressive depth at running back to actually bench Jonathan Taylor ... but it's also been the right decision more often than not lately. Amidst the Colts' midseason fire sale, Taylor has lost significant volume and struggled for fantasy. He's logged fewer than seven fantasy points in three of his last four games, with zero touchdowns and two fumbles lost over that span.

    Industry observers note that from Weeks 1-7, he averaged 23.7 opportunities per game (third in the league) ... but from Weeks 8-11, he dropped to just 16.8 per game. He averaged just 9.1 points per game against the extremely soft Cowboys and Dolphins run defenses in Weeks 9 and 10 and draws a much tougher matchup with the Giants this Sunday. Fresh York is allowing the sixth-fewest fantasy points per game to running backs, with just four rushing touchdowns on the season (tied with the Jaguars for third-fewest).

    I don't foresee the move to Anthony Richardson Sr. helping this offense much — they've averaged 21.9 points per game in his 19 starts — and he's a threat to vulture a goal-line touchdown from Taylor as well. At the very least, the former RB1 is a fade in DFS ... but he's also worth avoiding in redraft lineups if you have options.

    It has been revealed that what to do ❓ I'd put Taylor in the same range as Pollard ... while he's tough to sit, he's a major risk for single-digit fantasy points and is far closer to RB25 (or lower) than RB15.

    Industry observers note that yeah, we've got some big names in this week's article. Similar to Pollard and Taylor at running back, Wilson has long been a good bet for "must-start" volume ... but things have changed a bit over the second half of this season. He's seen fewer than seven targets in three of the last five games, logged fewer than 45 receiving yards in all three of those contests and hasn't scored a touchdown since Week 5.

    It has been revealed that as a result, he's averaging just 7.8 fantasy points per game since Week 6 ... and his season-low of just 3.6 points came against the Miami Dolphins in Week 7. Wilson caught just two of three targets for 26 yards in that game. And it wasn't all that shocking: no defense has faced fewer targets per game to wide receivers than Miami (14.0) and they've allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per game to the position as a result. Geno Smith being active didn't help much last week — Wilson logged just three catches for 39 yards — and the prevalence of the run game and growing contributions from Adonai Mitchell have made Wilson far less reliable than he once was. With a floor in the low single digits and a realistic ceiling in the low teens, he should be actively avoided in typical leagues.

    What to do ❓ Wilson is a legitimate sit candidate, decently outside WR2 range in my book. I'd rather look to lesser names with better opportunities like KC Concepcion, Carnell Tate, Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams or Ladd McConkey.

    Keenan Allen had a strong first game with the 49ers, catching five of seven targets for 61 yards against the lackluster Cowboys defense. Then, he had an expectedly down game against the elite Vikings defense, with just three catches for 38 yards. Unfortunately, his outlook against the Seahawks this Sunday is much more likely to emulate the former than the latter.

    Seattle is one of very few teams allowing fewer fantasy points per game to wide receivers ... in fact, the Seahawks are No. 1 in that metric, allowing an absurdly low 16.9 PPG. Only one wideout has topped 11 fantasy points against Seattle since Week 6 (Luther Burden III), and only three have done so all year (also Mike Evans and Terry McLaurin). With Brock Purdy playing like he has been, he'll probably hit a big pass or two, and throw a touchdown or two, but those plays are much more likely to go to Evans, George Kittle, Christian McCaffrey and even Deebo Samuel Sr. Allen is likely to be the odd-man out in a tough matchup and should be benched in all formats.

    What to do ❓ Allen isn't even a good FLEX option this week, do whatever you can to bench him in Week 12 (and stow him away for better matchups in the playoffs).

    Kyle Pitts Sr. had a strong stretch in the middle of the season that convinced fantasy managers that he was a reliable TE1 once again. It was a mirage. Over the last three weeks, he's totaled just 10.4 fantasy points, and even when he scored 10.7 back in Week 7 (thanks to a touchdown), he managed just 22 receiving yards. Outside of that trio of games from Weeks 5-7, he's logged fewer than five catches, 50 or fewer yards and zero touchdowns in every other week this season.

    In a recent development, and if the inconsistency wasn't enough to turn you away, the matchup with the Vikings should be. They've allowed the second-fewest fantasy points per game to the position (7.8) and had held every tight end they'd faced to single-digit fantasy points until Kittle scored a pair of touchdowns last week (on just three catches and 34 yards, by the way). Barring an extremely lucky touchdown, Pitts will be a massive bust once again in Week 12. Not the kind of bet you want to make amid a playoff push.

    What to do ❓ Sit Pitts for just about any viable streaming option. That list includes guys like Chig Okonkwo, Mike Gesicki, Brenton Strange and possibly even Dalton Schultz (if healthy) or Darren Waller.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, veteran right-handed starter Freddy Peralta has signed with the Baltimore Orioles on a five-year deal, the team confirmed on Tuesday. The contract is worth $125 million with no deferrals or options, The Athletic reports.

    Peralta, who will be going into his age-31 season in 2027, is coming off a campaign in which he didn't pitch up to his usual standards during a disastrous stint with the New York Mets. However, he did more like his old self following a deadline trade to the Tampa Bay Rays. On the Rays' watch, Peralta made a series of adjustments that helped him find better results on the mound, including being named the ALCS MVP.

    In a recent development, earlier this offseason, CBS Sports ranked Peralta as the No. 7 free agent of the 2026-27 class. Here's part of our write-up:.

    "It has been a roller coaster year for Peralta, who flopped with the Mets, rebounded with the Rays, then faced the Brewers (his former team) in the World Series and lost. The post-deadline stint with Tampa salvaged Peralta's free agent year. They made several adjustments, most notably raising his arm angle and getting him to pitch exclusively from the stretch, and the result was a livelier fastball and also better command. He's still five-and-fly Freddy. Even the best version of Peralta won't pitch deep into games and can be a tough watch because he nibbles and throws so many pitches per inning. They tend to be good innings, though, and the guy never misses a start. Worst case, Peralta is a mid-rotation starter you can count on to take the ball every fifth day. The best case is someone who can front a contender's rotation. Fastball Freddy was always going to be a great bounceback candidate this offseason. The Rays just beat everyone to it at the trade deadline.".

    Sources indicate that peralta isn't far removed from a 2023-25 stretch for the Milwaukee Brewers that saw him top 30 starts and 200 strikeouts in three straight seasons. In 2025, he earned his second All-Star selection and finished fifth in the National League Cy Young vote.

    "Freddy has proven to be a winning player who understands what it takes to compete and succeed on the biggest stage," noted Orioles president of baseball operations Mike Elias said in a statement. "His professionalism, preparation, and commitment to winning will set a strong example for our organization and we believe he will have a significant impact on our team both on and off the field.".

    Industry observers note that after losing Trevor Rogers to free agency (he agreed to a five-year contract with the Chicago Cubs earlier on Tuesday), the Orioles were searching for a new frontline starter to join a rotation that includes Kyle Bradish, Shane Baz and some combination of Brandon Young, Cade Povich and Trey Gibson. Elias has been hesitant to pay up for pitchers recently, but either his strategy has changed or he decided Peralta was worth the cost.

    The Orioles' disappointing fourth-place AL East finish in 2026 has raised questions about the state of Baltimore's rebuild, particularly amid stalled growth from its promising young position players, including Jackson Holliday, Gunnar Henderson and Colton Cowser. Would-be franchise backstop Adley Rutschman was traded to the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline.

    Because Peralta was traded during the 2026 season and was thus ineligible for the qualifying offer, the Orioles will not be penalized a draft pick for signing him.

    #222384. MLB rumors: Corey Seager willing to waive his NTC for Phillies, plus news on Mets, Nationals, Yankees, more

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1178 w)

    MLB rumors: Corey Seager willing to waive his NTC for Phillies, plus news on Mets, Nationals, Yankees, more

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway.
    • Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing.
    • Free agent catcher Tyler Stephenson has agreed to a three-year contract to return to the Reds, reports ESPN.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples. Just recently, for instance, the Fresh York Mets landed the biggest fish in the pond by signing ace Tarik Skubal to a record contract. Not long after, the Chicago Cubs fortified their rotation with Trevor Rogers and their outfield with Teruaki Sato, and Freddy Peralta is headed to the Baltimore Orioles. More's surely to come before lockout day arrives.

    Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Tuesday's supply just below.

    Free agent catcher Tyler Stephenson has agreed to a three-year contract to return to the Reds, reports ESPN. The deal is worth $30 million and includes an opt-out after the second year. Cincinnati selected Stephenson, 30, with the No. 11 pick in the 2015 draft, and he's played his entire career with the Reds. We ranked him as the 46th-best free agent available.

    Recent findings suggest that the Reds will again pair Stephenson with glove-first backup Jose Trevino behind the plate. Cincinnati now figures to turn their attention to the pitching staff, both the rotation and bullpen. Hunter Greene's UCL surgery means Andrew Abbott and Chase Burns are the only locks for the rotation, though Nick Lodolo will have a spot as long as he's healthy.

    It has been revealed that the Yankees are among the many teams with interest in top free agent reliever Adrian Morejon, reports the New York Post. Some teams view him as a potential starter, though there were reports earlier this month that he prefers to stay in the bullpen. The Phillies, meanwhile, are not considered a serious candidate to sign Morejon, according to The Athletic. We ranked him as the second-best free agent available this offseason, in part due to his potential to start.

    Adding to the bullpen has been the Yankees' primary focus so far this offseason. Closer David Bednar accepted the qualifying offer, they re-signed lefty matchup guy Tim Hill, and signed Jonathan Loáisiga and Tim Hill as free agents. At some point they will need to add to their lineup, particularly at third base, but there's always room for a reliever like Morejon in the bullpen.

    Recent findings suggest that the Philadelphia Phillies are open to moving Trea Turner off of shortstop given that he's now a pronounced defensive liability. Speaking of openness, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phillies and upgrade the position for them, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports.

    Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. Signed to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season (just before the last lockout, in fact), Seager is owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. The Rangers are reportedly looking to shake things up. The Phillies, meantime, are trying to keep their contention window open. It's a fit both ways, at least in theory. Such a move would likely mean a move to the outfield for Turner, who himself has very little trade value thanks to his ongoing decline and big contract.

    It has been revealed that even in a down 2026 year, Jazz Chisholm Jr. put up 19 homers and stole 41 bases while manning an up-the-middle position. Still just 28 years of age, he figures to have a healthy market this offseason. Speaking of which, the Washington Nationals are one of multiple teams presently in contact with Chisholm, FanSided reports.

    According to recent reports, earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Chisholm as the No. 6 free agent in the current class. Here's part of that write-up:.

    "In what was his worst season as a hitter since his rookie year in 2021, Chisholm was still a league-average bat in 2026, and his top-shelf defense and baserunning still landed him at 3.5 WAR. Chisholm is a style-over-substance player who is not for everyone, but his second base defense and near-MLB-best baserunning skills give him a very high floor. He's a reasonable bet for 20-ish home runs with the potential to go 30-30, and Chisholm has improved his plate discipline enough to run walk rates north of 10% the last two years. The downside is his propensity to swing and miss. Chisholm has posted below-average in-zone contact rates throughout his career and contact rates that low always come with risk. That risk is mitigated somewhat by the secondary skills (defense, etc.) and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29. You probably don't want him as your best or second-best player, but he's also an overqualified No. 6-7 hitter who brings so much else to the table.".

    The Cleveland Guardians have agreed to a free-agent contract with left-hander Kris Bubic, Sportsnet reports. The contract is for $17.5 million over one year, according to ESPN. Bubic, 29, made nine starts for the Kansas City Royals last season, and after the trade to the Los Angeles Dodgers, he was used out of the bullpen. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point, and he's an interesting "ceiling" candidate in the rotation. However, his substantial history of injuries may mean he's best used out of the bullpen.

    Sources indicate that the Detroit Tigers have added infield depth by agreeing to terms with Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year, $5 million free agent contract, ESPN reports. Kim, 31, is coming off a rough partial season with the Atlanta Braves, but he has a more palatable OPS+ of 91 for his career. He's been a primary shortstop in recent years and also has significant time spent at second base and third base.

    Industry observers note that even after achieving a reunion with veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray, the Minnesota Twins are still looking to fortify their roster for a return to contention in 2027. The club still hopes to make one more significant addition this offseason and add another player who may not grab as many headlines, the Athletic reports. Atop the wishlist are a first baseman or a second baseman and another lefty reliever.

    Even after the splash addition of Skubal, the Mets may not be done adding starting pitchers in the service of a rebound season in 2027. On that front, the Mets may be interested in adding a starting pitcher on a short-term deal for next season, the Athletic reports. That would likely limit them to the back half of the market, especially with so many bigger names reaching agreements.

    #222382. NBA rumors: Latest on Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns, plus Wizards' Anthony Davis plan, a Nets trade candidate

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1266 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    NBA rumors: Latest on Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns, plus Wizards' Anthony Davis plan, a Nets trade candidate

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we may be weeks away from the unofficial beginning of trade season on Dec.
    • Karl-Anthony Towns had a tense set of contract negotiations with the Newly introduced York Knicks last offseason, but if there was any fear that it would spill into his performance, those have quickly been squashed.
    • Technically speaking, the Knicks could still extend Towns during the season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we may be weeks away from the unofficial beginning of trade season on Dec. 15, but the NBA rumor mill has been surprisingly active. With a number of big names seemingly set for availability before February and a packed championship race, the next few transaction cycles figure to be loaded with movement. Let's dive into the latest batch of rumors.

    Karl-Anthony Towns had a tense set of contract negotiations with the Newly introduced York Knicks last offseason, but if there was any fear that it would spill into his performance, those have quickly been squashed. Towns, frankly, has been New York's best player this season. He's the NBA's rebounding leader, has maintained his defensive improvement from last season and the uptick in his playmaking that came in the playoffs, and of course, he's averaging a very efficient 22 points per game or so for a defending champion that has won five games in a row.

    Technically speaking, the Knicks could still extend Towns during the season. Multi-year contracts cannot be extended once the season has begun, but Towns could sign an extension by declining his $61 million player option for next year. However, there's little indication that the Knicks have changed their stance on wanting Towns to take a meaningful discount from his max on his next deal. "The Knicks, I think, would lose him if he opted out this summer and went into free agency," SNY's Ian Begley even stated on "The Putback.".

    In a recent development, now, we can qualify this as something closer to informed speculation than hard reporting. There is also plenty of time for things to change, either for the Knicks to offer more money or for circumstances to change in such a way that Towns would take less. If the Knicks win another championship, that certainly helps his case.

    The point that Begley is making here is that Towns is almost certain to receive substantial interest in free agency this offseason, with plenty of teams likely eager to pay him after the start he's had. If the Knicks were willing to increase their offer to a suitable level, well, this could be done already. A number of notable teams led by the Golden State Warriors could create substantial cap space this offseason. If one or more of these teams is willing to offer Towns the full max and the Knicks aren't, then yes, Newly introduced York would seemingly be in danger of losing its star significant man.

    Towns has reportedly been willing to sign for less than the max. There is simply a gulf between what he considers fair and what the Knicks have thus far been willing to offer. The Knicks drew a hard line in the sand about going above the second apron last offseason and it cost them backup center Mitchell Robinson. With new contracts for Jalen Brunson, OG Anunoby and Josh Hart also looming, the Knicks are pinching pennies even as the defending champion. There's still plenty of time for the two sides to find a middle ground here, but for now at least, it doesn't seem like Towns' strong start has changed much on New York's end.

    According to recent reports, there was a widespread assumption for a good chunk of the offseason that the Washington Wizards got Anthony Davis to flip him. He's 33. They didn't extend him when they had the chance in August. The drawn-out nature of LeBron James' free agency led plenty to believe he was trying to engineer a reunion with his former Los Angeles Lakers teammate. Alas, no deal came. When the Wizards started 4-11, the rumors picked back up.

    Industry observers note that and yet again, Washington's plans for Davis remain unclear. Reporting for The Stein Line, Jake Fischer noted that while several league cap strategists have told him they expect Davis to be traded, he has received pushback to the idea and does not believe, for now, that any trade is imminent. We are of course in peak posturing season. Plenty can change between now and February. Yet Washington already resisted trading Davis through one transaction cycle. A second doesn't seem out of the realm of possibility.

    Davis is in the middle of a renaissance season. He's averaging over 25 points and nearly 10 rebounds a game for a floundering Wizards team with minimal spacing. Still, his age and injury-proneness make him an enormously risky extension bet. Even in the best-case scenarios, it's unlikely that he remains a star-level player by the time Washington's young prospects are ready to contend seriously. Besides, with Trae Young's disastrous max contract on the books, extending Davis risks depriving Washington of any financial flexibility for the next several years. Couple that with the decline in Alex Sarr's usage when he shares the floor with Davis and there's plenty of reasonable motivation for Washington to pursue a trade. The longer they wait, the more they risk an injury that saps his value.

    Industry observers note that the Wizards gave up two first-round picks to get Davis, but they were weak ones: No. 30 overall last season, and a top 20 protected pick that is mathematically unlikely to actually convey. For now, they should be more than capable of turning Davis into a net asset profit by getting real draft capital for him. Yet the longer they hold out, the more believable the notion of keeping him actually becomes. With nothing realistically on the table from a salary perspective until at least Dec. 15, this sort of messaging early on makes plenty of sense. Whether the Wizards ultimately do keep Davis in the long run remains to be seen.

    From one player who has lasted longer with his current team than expected to another, Michael Porter Jr. was one of the more obvious trade candidates of the 2025-26 season. The Brooklyn Nets were tanking. He had a career year. Flipping him to a contender was the obvious move. But the Nets are notoriously patient when it comes to such trades. They held out longer than expected on Mikal Bridges and Cam Johnson and netted better packages for both than anyone could have imagined.

    Recent findings suggest that but they don't have that sort of time with Porter, who is in the last year of his contract and whose numbers have slipped back closer to their norms after last year's breakout. Unsurprisingly, he is a name that has featured heavily in the early season rumor mill, and the Fresh York Post reported Tuesday that the expectation is that he is indeed moved. "Michael Porter is a pending unrestricted free agent. As one still unsigned to an extension, he's widely expected by league personnel to be dealt by the trade deadline," Brian Lewis wrote.

    Porter, by virtue of his strong 3-point shooting, should be a relatively comfortable fit on most teams offensively. He was heavily linked to the Detroit Pistons last trade deadline, but no specific suitors have yet emerged as latest destinations this year. His $40.8 million cap figure will be tricky to trade, but if he and a new possible team are on the same page about the basic framework of a long-term deal, that's not an insurmountable problem. The Nets traded for Julius Randle at power forward in the offseason and have a number of young shot-creators to develop. If they viewed Porter as a major part of their future, they could have used cap space to renegotiate and extend him last offseason. They didn't, and now he's an obvious trade candidate for February.

    #222381. Industry News: Dylan Larkin trade grades: Red Wings notch massive win in blockbuster NHL deal with Canadiens

    Industry News: Dylan Larkin trade grades: Red Wings notch massive win in blockbuster NHL deal with Canadiens

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams confirmed on Sunday.
    • According to recent reports, in addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal.
    • Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams confirmed on Sunday. This deal ends a bitter saga between Larkin and the Red Wings, and Montreal gave up a king's ransom to make it happen.

    According to recent reports, in addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal. The Red Wings received forward Kirby Dach, goaltender Sam Montembeault, prospect Michael Hage, first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-round pick.

    Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day. As training camp opened in September, Detroit confirmed that Larkin had been stripped of his captaincy, and Larkin was booed by fans on opening night at Little Caesars Arena.

    After recovering from an injury he suffered in camp, Larkin played 10 games before announcing that he would be sitting out in anticipation of the trade. While sitting out, Larkin racked up major fines, but his trade request has finally been granted.

    Industry observers note that when he's on the ice, there's no denying that Larkin can make a significant impact. The 30-year-old Larkin just notched 34 goals and 33 assists for the Red Wings last season -- his fifth straight year hitting the 30-goal mark -- and he was instrumental in Team USA ending its lengthy gold medal drought at the 2026 Olympics.

    Industry observers note that in his career, Larkin has totaled 278 goals and 371 assists in 818 games. The first game Larkin — a native of Waterford, Michigan — plays for the Habs will also be the first he's ever played for a team based outside the Wolverine State.

    Industry observers note that larkin will give the Canadiens much-needed center depth, and he'll be under contract for a while. He's in the fourth year of an eight-year contract that pays him $8.7 million per season.

    According to recent reports, this trade fills a void that's existed in the Canadiens' lineup for several years now. Nick Suzuki has evolved into a legitimate star and a franchise-caliber No. 1 center. Beyond him, Montreal has struggled to find a true second-line center.

    Larkin absolutely fits that bill. While he was a bit miscast in Detroit as a first-line center, Larkin is one of the best No. 2 options in the NHL, and he gives the Canadiens an elite one-two punch down the middle.

    Industry observers note that did the Canadiens overpay a bit for a 30-year-old second-line center? In a vacuum, they did. However, taken in context, this deal makes plenty of sense for the Habs.

    Recent findings suggest that montreal's championship window is just now opening. It already has an elite young core locked up for the next several seasons on team-friendly deals. Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Ivan Demidov, Juraj Slafkovsky, Lane Hutson and Noah Dobson are all 27 or younger and make less than $10 million per season.

    In a recent development, that gives general manager Kent Hughes a bit more freedom to be aggressive on the trade market. Picks and prospects are nice, but they don't do much good for a team looking to make the jump to contender status in 2026-27. Besides, the Canadiens have been building their prospect pool for years now. It's time to flip some of those assets for proven star power.

    The Canadiens paid a premium to acquire Larkin. There's no two ways about it. However, Montreal fills a major need and looks a lot more formidable in the Eastern Conference. The Stanley Cup window is officially wide open for the ascending Canadiens. Grade -- B+.

    Consider the situation interim general manager Shawn Horcoff faced. Everyone knew that Larkin wanted out of Detroit so badly that he was paying not to play for the Red Wings.

    On top of that, Larkin had a full no-trade clause, and his list of approved teams amounted to no more than a dozen.

    Should I also mention that Horcoff was thrust into this role in the midst of the offseason, when franchise legend Steve Yzerman was effectively fired for mishandling the Wings' rebuild?

    Given all of that, it's hard to see this as anything less than a home run for Detroit. In fact, it's probably more like a grand slam. Not only did the Red Wings get multiple first-round picks and a couple useful NHL players out of the deal, but they also landed a legitimate blue-chip prospect in Hage.

    The No. 21 pick in the 2024 NHL Draft, Hage is off to a roaring start at the University of Michigan this season with five goals and 21 assists in just 13 games. Detroit might have replaced one franchise center with another one, assuming Hage continues to develop at this rate.

    This was a great piece of work from Horcoff, who probably just made a strong case for the full-time general manager gig in Detroit. This haul will allow the Wings to kickstart another retool or swing a substantial trade to bolster the current roster. Either way, the outlook just got a lot brighter in Hockeytown. Grade -- A+.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a newly introduced collective bargaining agreement.
    • In a recent development, the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years.
